pages.text: Tori Kelly: Tiny Desk Concert : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Tori Kelly: Tiny Desk Concert Not only does Tori Kelly fill the Tiny Desk with her commanding voice but also genuine joy and light. Tori Kelly: Tiny Desk Concert September 10, 2026 5:00 AM ET Ashley Pointer Credit: Photo: Michael Zamora/NPR When Tori Kelly pulled up to the Desk, her band already mid-rehearsal, she immediately got to work and filled our room with her commanding voice. She had arrived. And with her, she carried genuine joy and light. Backed by an all-woman band of Tiny Desk alumnae, Kelly effortlessly moves through songs from her latest album, God Must Really Love Me . The record captures Kelly in the present: reflecting on her faith journey and navigating life as a new mom. She also drops some gems for the day one's, including brief tastes of "Nobody Love" and "Dear No One." But, most serendipitously for the middle schoolers in attendance, Kelly performs her rendition of Stevie Wonder 's "Don't You Worry 'Bout a Thing," the song that her character Meena belts in the animated film Sing . Sponsor Message I've always found Tori Kelly to be inspiring. Beyond her anointing as a vocalist and musician, she has endured the many shifts of the music industry while maintaining an authenticity that cuts through the noise and reaches the heart. There's something special about watching an artist who has grown so much, yet still sounds and feels unmistakably like herself. pages.description: Winding through the Southern Alps in New Zealand, the TranzAlpine is lauded as one of the world’s greatest rail journeys, but few know that its well-worn tracks also trace the path of an ancestral Māori trade route.
pages.text: Tracing Māori jade culture along the TranzAlpine rail route in New Zealand | National Geographic By Justin Meneguzzi Published November 2, 2025 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Te Rua Mason believes finding pounamu is much like finding love. Despite the spitting rain and biting wind, Te Rua, his son Henare and I are picking our way along the pebbled mouth of the Arahura River outside Hokitika township. The steel-grey Tasman Sea crashes and foams against the shore nearby, hurling salty spray into the air. Sky-wheeling seagulls bicker and caw. The weather might be dreary but Te Rua, my guide and founder of Te Rua and Sons Pounamu Trail tours, says it’s a good day to search for pounamu, a type of jade found exclusively on the west coast of New Zealand’s South Island. Too much sunlight can wash everything in an indiscernible glare — rain helps the stone’s natural green stand out among the limestone and quartz. Even with the weather’s help, finding pounamu is a fated encounter, a bit like meeting your soulmate — if it’s meant to be, the stone will find you. Today, it seems, I’m unlucky in love. I show Te Rua an emerald-coloured rock the size of a large apple, but he says the colour is just algae. “Practice makes perfect,” he assures me. An imposing figure with an intricate facial moko (a sacred tattoo that represents his Māori ancestry), my gently spoken guide opens up about his connection to the river as we walk. pages.text: Tracking a Mystery: When and How the First Americans Arrived | National Geographic The Oregon Coast, pictured here, may have been a byway for the first Americans as they followed the nutrient-rich coast southward on foot and by boat, says the new book, Atlas of a Lost World . Photograph by Ty Milford, Aurora BOOK TALK When, How Did the First Americans Arrive? It’s Complicated. The first Americans weren't one group of people; they arrived at different times, and likely by different methods. By Simon Worrall Published June 9, 2018 • 13 min read How did human beings first come to North America? Across the Bering Strait, on foot? Down the “kelp highway” by boat? Across the Atlantic via the polar ice cap? And when did they reach here? 10,000 years ago? 40,000? Or were they always here, as the Navajo and other Native American tribes believe? In his new book, Atlas Of A Lost World , author Craig Childs sets off to test these different theories on the ground, traveling from Alaska to Chile, Canada to Florida. What he finds, despite the best efforts of archaeologists and the latest technology , still remains in many ways a mystery. Speaking from his home in Colorado, he explains why many Native Americans reject the idea that their ancestors migrated from somewhere else; how an archaeologist nicknamed Dr. Poop believes he has identified the first human excrement in America ; and why diversity seems to have been built into America’s DNA. Treatment of Pertussis For Health Care Providers Aug. 25, 2026 Key points Treatment within the first 1-2 weeks is most effective for reducing symptom severity. Healthcare providers should consider treating prior to test results if certain circumstances are present. Choosing the type of antibiotic to use may depend on a number of factors, including age and antibiotic resistance patterns. Find more information below about who to treat, when to treat, and antibiotic selection. Early treatment can reduce severity The earlier someone, especially an infant, starts treatment the better. See a healthcare provider if you or your child has symptoms of whooping cough. Treatment Healthcare providers generally treat whooping cough with antibiotics. There are several antibiotics available for treatment. It's very important to treat whooping cough early , before coughing fits begin. Ralf Blank / Hagener Stadtgeschichte Last month, a history teacher cleaning his aunt’s house in Hagen, Germany, after severe flooding discovered a trove of Nazi artifacts hidden behind a wall, reports David Crossland for the London Times . “I got goosebumps,” Sebastian Yurtseven told local media, as quoted by the Times . “I didn’t think it would turn into such a huge discovery.” When Yurtseven pulled out a rotten piece of plasterboard, he spotted a foot-wide space behind the wall containing a newspaper dated to 1945, writes Insider ’s Sophia Ankel. Investigating further, he found a cache of World War II–era artifacts, including a portrait of Adolf Hitler, a revolver, gas masks, Nazi Party badges, brass knuckles, letters and documents. As it turns out, the building housed the local headquarters of the National Socialist People’s Welfare organization (NSV) during the Nazi era. Yurtseven and his aunt say the family had no idea of this history when they purchased the property in the 1960s. Ralf Blank , manager of the Hagen city archive , tells Frankfurter Allgemeine that NSV members probably hid the documents and other materials in the wall when Allied troops marched into the city in April 1945. “That must have happened very hectically,” he says. TSCA Section 21 Under TSCA section 21, any person may petition EPA to initiate a proceeding for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule or order under: Section 4 -- rules or orders requiring chemical testing; Section 6 -- rules imposing regulatory controls on chemicals; Section 8 -- rules requiring information; or Section 5(e) or (f) -- orders affecting new chemical substances. The petition must be filed in EPA's Office of the Administrator and set forth the facts that are claimed to establish the necessity for the action requested. EPA is required to grant or deny the petition within 90 days from the day the petition is filed with EPA. If EPA grants the petition, EPA must promptly commence an appropriate proceeding. If EPA denies the petition, the reasons for denial must be published in the Federal Register. Close Turiy's Diary Комбинации тэгов для обозначения велосипедных дорожек Posted by Turiy on 8 October 2026 in Russian (Русский) . Last updated on 9 October 2026. Обозначение обособленной велосипедной дорожки: highway=cycleway - основной тег линии, который указывает, что путь предназначен для движения на велосипедах. foot=no - явно запрещает движение пешеходов (если пешеходам запрещено находиться на этой дорожке). Если пешеходы разрешены, но дорожка разделена на зоны, используют foot=yes и segregated=yes/no . Велосипедная дорожка + тротуар: Комбинация тэгов для обозначения пешеходного тротуара, совмещённого с выделенной велосипедной дорожкой, которая конструктивно или визуально отделена от пешеходной зоны: highway=footway - обозначает, что данный объект является обустроенной дорожкой, предназначенной в первую очередь для пешеходов. footway=sidewalk - уточняет тип пешеходной дорожки. Этот тег указывает, что дорожка является тротуаром, то есть идет параллельно автомобильной дороге (обычно повторяя её геометрию). bicycle=designated - указывает на официальный юридический статус для велосипедистов. Это значит, что дорожка специально выделена/предназначена для движения на велосипеде (например, установлен соответствующий знак или нанесена разметка), а не просто «разрешена для транзита». segregated=yes - означает, что потоки пешеходов и велосипедистов разделены. Dakota (instead called Lakota by speakers of that dialect ) is the indigenous language of the Oc̣eṭi Ṡakowiƞ (Seven Council Fires) people of North America, consisting of the Bdewaḳaƞṭuƞwaƞ, Waḣpeḳute, Waḣpeṭuƞwaƞ, Sisiṭuƞwaƞ, Ihaƞkṭuƞwaƞ, Ihaƞkṭuƞwaƞna and Ṭiṭuƞwaƞ communities. Most members of these communities will describe themselves as Dakota (or Lakota for the Ṭiṭuƞwaƞ) people. Dakota and Lakota communities can be found in Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Montana, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. All of these places have a rich geography of names devised by Oc̣eṭi Ṡakowiƞ people in the Dakota/Lakota language, including rivers, lakes, towns, islands, hills and more. People have traveled since the dawn of human history and some areas once had Dakota/Lakota communities that presently do not, and so other areas (such as Wisconsin, Iowa, Wyoming and Ontario) also have locations with names in the language. Historically, there have been far, far more Dakota and Lakota place names than those that survive for us to learn about them in the present. When assigning Dakota and Lakota names to map elements, I am mainly drawing on the (often lifelong) work of others; very few of my changes are based on personal local knowledge. I have focused on sources who are either directly part of, or at least worked closely with, authentic Oc̣eti Ṡakowiƞ communities. This is the language of nations that are alive today, and they have things to say! My major sources include: My mapping work owes an enormous amount to (and sits in the shadow of) the absolutely incredible Maḳoc̣e Waṡte map by Lakota historian Dakota Wind Goodhouse, who drew on a vast range of sources to populate the names of thousands of places. His blog The First Scout is one of the best public history projects you’ll find anywhere, and you should check it out. Sometimes my research has led me to different conclusions on the precise meaning and pronunciation of some place names, and the largest limitation of his map is the one he tells you about right away (it is a Landscape Map and so rarely discusses towns and cities) but this is still the single largest, most thorough map of Lakota/Dakota place names you will find anywhere until such time as I can somehow map twice as much content as I have. pages.text: Tuwewanzi's Diary | Dakota/Lakota Dialects | OpenStreetMap Select Language Loading... Close Tuwewanzi's Diary Dakota/Lakota Dialects Posted by Tuwewanzi on 12 November 2026 in English . Last updated on 17 November 2026. My mapping on OpenStreetMap includes names in both Dakota and Lakota, with ISO codes dak and lkt respectively. This is an unusual approach compared to a lot of other multilingual mapping, so it’s worth explaining in more detail. Dakota and Lakota are two different dialects of the same language (and are two possible names for that language). They are mutually intelligible, and a fluent speaker of one can understand a fluent speaker of the other without difficulty. An analogy might be made to the Spanish spoken in Mexico vs the Spanish spoken in Spain - a speaker of the other dialect will seem to have a strong accent, unusual pronunciation, and some different word choices, but they are still clearly speaking your language . Both dialects are endangered, but there are substantially more Lakota speakers than Dakota speakers and this has been true for a long time. Dakota and Lakota share the vast majority of their vocabulary. Most words that differ between these dialects differ in predictable, formulaic ways that do not represent any difference in meaning (e.g. Oṭuƞwe vs Otȟúŋwahe or Bde vs Ble). The most meaningful differences in Lakota vs Dakota speech emerge in conversational flow, which rarely matters for place names. Close Tuwewanzi's Diary Dakota/Lakota Writing Systems and Orthography Posted by Tuwewanzi on 12 November 2026 in English . The Dakota/Lakota language has been a written language for only the most recent chapters of its history. Writing systems for the language were first devised by 19th-century missionaries who sought to promote literacy as a part of encouraging Dakota people to convert to Christianity. These missionaries, especially Stephen Riggs , developed an alphabet based on the Latin Alphabet to represent the sounds present in the language. All widely used methods for writing the language today are based on Riggs’ system with some degree of variation. There is no single writing system accepted by the vast majority of speaker communities. A variety of systems - or orthographies - exist with varying degrees of popularity, and invididual speakers and teachers often have strong preferences one way or another. Areas of debate include: May an orthography make use of special characters (ŋ, ǧ, ḳ, ú) or should writing be done only with characters that can be written with a standard English keyboard? The language contains vowels (a, i, u) that may be nasalized or not, depending on context; should the orthography note the difference? The language contains consonants (z, c, p, t, k, s) that may be aspirated for a harder sound or unaspirated; should the orthography note the difference? pages.title: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback
pages.description: Long thought to have been looted from northern England by Scottish tribes, the larger-than-life leg may have actually been displayed in Roman Scotland, before it was carefully dismantled and buried by retreating forces
pages.text: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback Skip to main content Curator Fraser Hunter examines the bronze leg. Duncan McGlynn In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops. “This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement . The bronze leg shows no signs of being violently hacked off the larger statue. Types of Diphtheria Vaccines For Everyone July 31, 2026 Español Key points Diphtheria vaccines are combined with tetanus and sometimes whooping cough (pertussis) vaccines. Diphtheria vaccines work well but protection decreases over time. Due to vaccination, diphtheria is now nearly unheard of in the United States. Although T. rex is a household name, what we know about this tyrannosaur is constantly evolving. Improved technologies, such as biomechanical modeling and x-ray imaging, have allowed scientists to gain a deeper understanding of how this apex predator lived. This dinosaur’s muscular body stretched as long as 40 feet—about the size of a school bus —from its snout to the tip of its powerful tail. Weighing up to eight tons, T. rex stomped headfirst across its territory on two strong legs. What’s your earliest travel memory? Going to the south of France. My parents used to drive straight down from London to Nice, sometimes in one 17-hour road trip. We’d listen to my dad’s audiobooks and watch cartoons in the back. I remember spending time in different parts of the south, going through olive trees and to the ocean. I was at my bookworm peak, so I’d always go out to a field or tuck myself away in a corner of the house to read. Do you have a favourite place in the world? São Paulo in Brazil. I loved wandering the streets, getting lost, exploring street markets. I went dancing in clubs with these little local bands of 70-year-old men who’d been playing in jazz outfits since they were 20. We honor privacy, protect confidentiality, share our expertise globally, and conduct our work openly. We are guided on this mission by scientific objectivity, our strong and capable workforce, our devotion to research-based innovation, and our abiding commitment to our customers. Our History Thomas Jefferson directed the first census in 1790. As required by the U.S. Constitution, a census has been taken every 10 years thereafter. In 1840, the Census Act authorized the establishment of a centralized Census Office. In 1902, the Census Office became a permanent organization within the Department of the Interior. A year later, it was renamed the Bureau of the Census and moved to the new Department of Commerce and Labor.
